messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame was twelve when the kitchen became a battlefield he could not stop. He remembered the exact cadence of his father’s boots on the linoleum, the sharp crack of a plate against the wall, his mother’s muffled sobs behind a partially closed door. Kwame had stood in the hallway, fists clenched, convinced that if he only found the right words or stepped forward, he could halt it. He had not moved. The violence never stopped, and the image of his own paralysis had calcified over decades. Over the years, Kwame had come to believe that safety was a fragile promise. Even when his partner, Elena, would trace his back and whisper that he was safe now, he found it impossible to believe it. During the harvest season, his work on the farm became a series of quiet calculations. He could not tolerate sitting in the tractor cab alone with a coworker; he was certain that isolation would be his undoing, so he would insist on keeping a radio on or texting Elena constantly until someone answered. At night, the farmhouse grew heavy. Kwame found it harder to feel safe after dusk. He would pace the hallway, listen for every creak, his body locked in a state of watchfulness, scanning the perimeter long after the other house lights went out. When Elena finally fell asleep, he stayed awake, his mind circling the same old thoughts: if he had been older, stronger, what would he have done to the man who broke the kitchen, and how might he still get even? The thoughts did not fade; they sharpened. He had come to understand that trying to suppress them only made the edges more jagged, so he focused on the dirt under his fingernails or the rhythm of the irrigation pumps, trying hard not to think about what happened. The farm demanded long hours, but Kwame’s days were measured in scans. He walked the rows with his shoulders tight, reading the treeline and the sky for trouble. His foreman had noticed the way Kwame flinched at sudden radio static or the slam of a gate, but Kwame only worked harder, taking on the late-night equipment checks that left him exhausted. The distance between him and Elena grew quietly. She would leave plates of food cooling on the counter, wondering why he would not let her sit with him in the living room after dinner. He needed to know someone was in the next room. The man who used to laugh at county fairs and hum gospel hymns had vanished, replaced by a quiet misery that felt as permanent as the harvest cycles. He had lost his faith in people, in the orderly way of things, and in any higher power that might have watched the kitchen that night and done nothing. Worse, he would never forgive himself for standing there, frozen, while the plates broke and his mother’s shoulders shook. The breaking point came in late August, when a backhoe overturned a section of the irrigation line. The metal groaned, steam hissed, and for a terrifying second, Kwame was twelve again, trapped in the doorway as the world spun out of control. He dropped his clipboard and stumbled backward, his breath coming in short, sharp pulls until Elena found him by the drip tape, her hands on his arms, telling him it was just a machine, just water, just now. He leaned into her grip, exhausted by the constant weight of staying alert, tired of the long nights, tired of carrying the quiet revenge fantasies that kept him company in the dark. He had finally called the clinic, hoping to find a way to sleep through the night without bracing for impact, hoping someone could help him stop replaying the kitchen in his head, hoping to reclaim the man he used to be before the violence taught him that the world was always one raised voice away from danger.
